content.prompt: Points labelled O in this exercise are always centres of circles.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Use compasses to draw a large circle with centre O, and draw a diameter AOB.

answer.short: Sample construction: a circle with centre O and diameter AOB.
answer.worked: Set the compasses to a fixed positive radius and draw a circle centred at O. Draw a straight line through O to meet the circle at A and B. The completed construction in the next part retains this diameter.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Draw an angle ∠APB in one of the semicircles. What is its size?

answer.worked: Choose a point P on either semicircle, distinct from A and B, and join PA and PB. Since AB is a diameter, Thales’ theorem gives $\angle APB=90^\circ$.

spec.description: Editable sample circle, diameter through centre and apex on semicircle; perpendicular AP/PB and explicit rightangle construction, no fixed size required.
spec.mathematics: Editable sample circle, diameter through centre and apex on semicircle; perpendicular AP/PB and explicit rightangle construction, no fixed size required.
spec.answerVisibility: Sample answer only; no original student given added.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Draw another large circle, and draw a chord AB that is not a diameter.

answer.short: Sample construction: a circle with a chord AB that does not pass through O.
answer.worked: Draw another circle and mark two points A and B that are not opposite ends of a diameter. Join AB. Retain this drawing for the two comparisons below.

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Draw the angle at the centre and an angle at the circumference subtended by the minor arc AB. How are these two angles related?

answer.short: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same minor arc AB.
answer.worked: Join OA and OB, marking the smaller central angle. Choose a point P on the major arc and join PA and PB, so both angles stand on the minor arc AB. The centre–circumference theorem gives $\angle AOB=2\angle APB$. In the sample completed drawing below these angles are $120^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.

children.label: v
children.prompt: Mark the angle at the centre on the major arc AB and draw an angle at the circumference subtended by this major arc. How are these two angles related?

answer.short: The reflex angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same major arc AB.
answer.worked: Mark the reflex central angle between OA and OB. Choose a point Q on the minor arc and join QA and QB; both angles now stand on the major arc AB. The same theorem applies: reflex $\angle AOB=2\angle AQB$. In the sample, the reflex central angle is $240^\circ$ and $\angle AQB=120^\circ$.

content.prompt: Find the values of $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\theta$, giving reasons.

spec.description: AB diameter through O; P on circle, original PAB15degree external leader, alphaAPB and betaPBA.
spec.mathematics: AB diameter through O; P on circle, original PAB15degree external leader, alphaAPB and betaPBA.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original angle givens and unknown Greek labels; answers remain in editable answer fields.

answer.worked: AB is a diameter, so $\alpha=\angle APB=90^\circ$ (Thales). The triangle angle sum gives $\beta=180^\circ-90^\circ-15^\circ=75^\circ$.

spec.description: PQ diameter through O, given QPT65, thetaPTQ.
spec.mathematics: PQ diameter through O, given QPT65, thetaPTQ.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original angle givens and unknown Greek labels; answers remain in editable answer fields.

answer.worked: PQ is a diameter, so the angle subtended at T is a right angle by Thales: $\theta=90^\circ$.

spec.description: JK diameter; KJL80, thetaJKL.
spec.mathematics: JK diameter; KJL80, thetaJKL.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original angle givens and unknown Greek labels; answers remain in editable answer fields.

answer.worked: The angle JLK is $90^\circ$ because JK is a diameter. Therefore $\theta=180^\circ-90^\circ-80^\circ=10^\circ$.

spec.description: RS diameter through O; RST70degree given, alphaTOS thetaROT betaRTO gammaOTS.
spec.mathematics: RS diameter through O; RST70degree given, alphaTOS thetaROT betaRTO gammaOTS.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original angle givens and unknown Greek labels; answers remain in editable answer fields.

answer.worked: OS=OT are radii, so $\gamma=\angle OTS=\angle OST=70^\circ$. Hence $\alpha=180^\circ-2(70^\circ)=40^\circ$. Since R,O,S are collinear, $\theta=180^\circ-40^\circ=140^\circ$. Finally OR=OT, so $\beta=(180^\circ-140^\circ)/2=20^\circ$.

spec.description: XY diameter through O, ZOY70 given, alphaOZY and betaZXY.
spec.mathematics: XY diameter through O, ZOY70 given, alphaOZY and betaZXY.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original angle givens and unknown Greek labels; answers remain in editable answer fields.

answer.worked: OZ=OY, so the base angles of triangle ZOY are equal: $\alpha=(180^\circ-70^\circ)/2=55^\circ$. The angle at X subtends the same minor arc ZY as the central angle $70^\circ$, so $\beta=70^\circ/2=35^\circ$.

spec.description: AB diameter through O; minor central COB160, thetaOAC, no additional numeric given.
spec.mathematics: AB diameter through O; minor central COB160, thetaOAC, no additional numeric given.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original angle givens and unknown Greek labels; answers remain in editable answer fields.

answer.worked: A,O,B are collinear, so $\angle AOC=180^\circ-160^\circ=20^\circ$. Since OA=OC, triangle AOC is isosceles and $\theta=(180^\circ-20^\circ)/2=80^\circ$.

spec.description: Reflex BOA200 shown left majorarc, C on complementary arc; gammaBCA.

content.prompt: Find the values of $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\theta$, giving reasons.

spec.description: Circle with centre O, chords PA and PB, and radii OA and OB. Alpha is the lower central angle; 240 degrees labels its reflex counterpart.
spec.mathematics: Reflex AOB=240 degrees; alpha=AOB; beta=APB.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=360^\circ-240^\circ\\\alpha&=120^\circ\\\beta&=\tfrac12\times120^\circ\\\beta&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles about a point sum to $360^\circ$. The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre standing on the same arc.

spec.description: Radii OA and OB and chords PA and PB; 300 degrees labels the reflex central sector.
spec.mathematics: Reflex AOB=300 degrees; theta=APB.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=360^\circ-300^\circ\\\angle AOB&=60^\circ\\\theta&=\tfrac12\times60^\circ\\\theta&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$
Use angles about a point, then the centre–circumference theorem on minor arc $AB$.

spec.description: Chords TS and TR and radii OS and OR; theta labels the reflex central sector to the left of O.
spec.mathematics: STR=70 degrees; theta is reflex SOR.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle SOR&=2\times70^\circ\\\angle SOR&=140^\circ\\\theta&=360^\circ-140^\circ\\\theta&=220^\circ\end{align*}$$
The minor central angle is twice $\angle STR$ on the same arc. Angles about $O$ sum to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Both unknown circumference angles stand on arc FG; beta is identified by an external leader.
spec.mathematics: FOG=80 degrees; alpha=FPG; beta=FQG.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=\tfrac12\times80^\circ=40^\circ\\\beta&=\tfrac12\times80^\circ=40^\circ\end{align*}$$
Each angle at the circumference stands on the same arc $FG$ as the $80^\circ$ central angle.

spec.description: Chords PS, PR, QS and QR and radii OS and OR; a leader gives angle SPR; theta labels reflex SOR.
spec.mathematics: SPR=20 degrees; alpha=SQR; theta is reflex SOR.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle SOR&=2\times20^\circ=40^\circ\\\theta&=360^\circ-40^\circ=320^\circ\\\alpha&=\tfrac12\times40^\circ=20^\circ\end{align*}$$
Use the centre–circumference theorem on arc $SR$ and angles about $O$.

spec.description: Triangle PRQ with radii OP, OR and OQ; unknown central sectors alpha and beta and angle RPO labelled gamma.
spec.mathematics: POQ=120 degrees; ORQ=40 degrees; alpha=ROQ; beta=ROP; gamma=RPO.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$OR=OQ$, so $\angle OQR=40^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=180^\circ-40^\circ-40^\circ=100^\circ\\\beta&=360^\circ-120^\circ-100^\circ=140^\circ\\\gamma&=\frac{180^\circ-140^\circ}{2}=20^\circ\end{align*}$$
Use the angle sum of $\triangle ROQ$, angles about $O$, and the equal base angles of $\triangle ROP$, where $OR=OP$.

spec.description: Quadrilateral BPAQ with radii OB and OA; alpha stands on the upper arc BA and gamma on the lower arc BA.
spec.mathematics: Minor BOA=160 degrees; beta is reflex BOA; alpha=BQA; gamma=BPA.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=\tfrac12\times160^\circ=80^\circ\\\beta&=360^\circ-160^\circ=200^\circ\\\gamma&=\tfrac12\times200^\circ=100^\circ\end{align*}$$
Each circumference angle is half the central angle standing on its arc. Angles about $O$ sum to $360^\circ$.

spec.description: Quadrilateral DABC with diameters AC and DB; source angle labels are retained on each side of the diameters.
spec.mathematics: DAC=30 degrees; alpha=CAB; beta=DBA; gamma=DBC.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$\angle DAB=90^\circ$ because $DB$ is a diameter.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ\\\beta&=\alpha=60^\circ\\\gamma&=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ\end{align*}$$
$OA=OB$, so the base angles of $\triangle AOB$ are equal. Also $\angle ABC=90^\circ$ because $AC$ is a diameter.

spec.description: Quadrilateral JKLM with perpendicular diameters JL and KM; right-angle square constructed from the radius vectors OK and OL.
spec.mathematics: KOL=90 degrees; alpha=KJL; beta=MKL.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:
$OJ=OK$ and $\angle JOK=90^\circ$, so $\triangle JOK$ is isosceles. Likewise $OK=OL$ and $\angle KOL=90^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=\frac{180^\circ-90^\circ}{2}=45^\circ\\\beta&=\frac{180^\circ-90^\circ}{2}=45^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Horizontal diameter AB and parallel chord FG; crossing chords AG and BF meet at M. A leader identifies beta at F.

spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

answer.worked:

spec.description: Diameter AB, radius OP and chords AP and BP; matching double ticks mark AO and AP.

spec.description: Radii OP and OQ, chords PR and QR, matching parallel arrows and a leader to angle QRP.

$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=20^\circ\\\gamma&=2\times20^\circ=40^\circ\\\beta&=40^\circ\end{align*}$$
$\alpha=20^\circ$ by alternate angles, since $OP\parallel QR$. The central angle $\gamma$ is twice $\angle QRP$ on arc $PQ$. Finally $\beta=\gamma$ by alternate angles, since $OP\parallel QR$.

spec.description: Quadrilateral OABC; alpha labels the reflex central angle, beta the angle at B and gamma the angle at C.
spec.mathematics: BAO=50 degrees; minor AOC=140 degrees; alpha is reflex AOC; beta=ABC; gamma=BCO.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=360^\circ-140^\circ=220^\circ\\\beta&=\tfrac12\times220^\circ=110^\circ\\\gamma&=360^\circ-140^\circ-50^\circ-110^\circ\\\gamma&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Radii OP and OR, chords PQ and QR, matching parallel arrows on PQ and OR; alpha labels the reflex central sector.
spec.mathematics: Lower POR=160 degrees; PQ parallel OR; beta=PQR; gamma=ORQ. Q is derived at 330 degrees so PQ is parallel to OR.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only.

$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=360^\circ-160^\circ=200^\circ\\\beta&=\tfrac12\times200^\circ=100^\circ\\\gamma&=180^\circ-100^\circ=80^\circ\end{align*}$$
Use angles about $O$, the centre–circumference theorem on major arc $PR$, and co-interior angles with $PQ\parallel OR$.

spec.description: Chords AB and AC and radii OB and OC; double ticks mark AB=BO; 200 degrees labels the right-hand reflex BOC sector.
spec.mathematics: Reflex BOC=200 degrees; alpha=BAC; beta=ABO; gamma=ACO.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and unknown labels only; auxiliary radius OA is reserved for the solution.

answer.short:
$\alpha=100^\circ$, $\beta=60^\circ$, $\gamma=40^\circ$.

Join $OA$ to identify an equilateral triangle.
answer.worked:
$$\alpha=\tfrac12\times200^\circ=100^\circ.$$
The circumference angle stands on the major arc $BC$.

Join $OA$. Since $OA=OB=AB$, $\triangle AOB$ is equilateral, so $\beta=60^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle BOC&=360^\circ-200^\circ=160^\circ\\\gamma&=360^\circ-160^\circ-100^\circ-60^\circ\\\gamma&=40^\circ\end{align*}$$
The interior angles of quadrilateral $ABOC$ sum to $360^\circ$.

content.prompt:
Thales’ theorem states that: An angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

This question develops two other proofs of Thales’ theorem. We must prove, in each part, that $\angle APB=90^\circ$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
(Euclid’s proof) Join $PO$, and produce $AP$ to $X$.

Let $\angle A=\alpha$ and $\angle B=\beta$.

spec.description: Diameter AB and chords AP, PB; dashed red constructions PO and PX, with A, P, X collinear. Ordinary geometry and point marker use house black.
spec.mathematics: O is the centre; A,O,B are collinear; A,P,X are collinear; alpha=PAB and beta=PBA.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and constructions only.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle APB=\alpha+\beta$, and that $\angle XPB=\alpha+\beta$.

answer.short:
$\angle APB=\angle XPB=\alpha+\beta$.

Use equal base angles in the two isosceles triangles and the exterior-angle theorem.
answer.worked:
$OA=OP$, so $\triangle AOP$ is isosceles and $\angle APO=\angle PAO=\alpha$.

$OB=OP$, so $\triangle BOP$ is isosceles and $\angle OPB=\angle PBO=\beta$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle APB&=\angle APO+\angle OPB\\\angle APB&=\alpha+\beta.\end{align*}$$
Since $AP$ is produced to $X$, the exterior-angle theorem in $\triangle APB$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\angle XPB&=\angle PAB+\angle PBA\\\angle XPB&=\alpha+\beta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence, prove that $\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$.

answer.short: $\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$, since the equal adjacent angles at $P$ form a straight angle.
answer.worked:
$A,P,X$ are collinear, so $\angle APB+\angle XPB=180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2(\alpha+\beta)&=180^\circ\\\alpha+\beta&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\angle APB=90^\circ$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Join $PO$ and produce it to $M$.

spec.description: Diameter AB and triangle APB, with dashed red diameter PM through O. Ordinary geometry and point marker use house black.
spec.mathematics: O is the centre; A,O,B and P,O,M are collinear; alpha=PAB and beta=PBA.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and constructions only.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle AOM=2\alpha$ and $\angle BOM=2\beta$.

answer.short:
$\angle AOM=2\alpha$ and $\angle BOM=2\beta$.

$A,O,B$ are collinear, so $\angle AOM+\angle MOB=180^\circ$.

$OP=OB$ because they are radii, so $\triangle OPB$ is isosceles and $\angle OPB=\angle PBO=\beta$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle AOB=2\beta$.

answer.short: $\angle AOB=2\beta$, by the exterior-angle theorem in $\triangle OPB$.
answer.worked:
$\angle AOB$ is an exterior angle of $\triangle OPB$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=\angle OPB+\angle PBO\\\angle AOB&=\beta+\beta\\\angle AOB&=2\beta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii

answer.short:
$\angle APB=\beta-\alpha$.

Subtract the base angles obtained from equal radii.
answer.worked:
$OA=OP$, so $\angle APO=\angle OAP=\alpha$.

$OB=OP$, so $\angle OPB=\angle PBO=\beta$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle APB&=\angle OPB-\angle OPA\\\angle APB&=\beta-\alpha.\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle AOB=2(\beta-\alpha)$.

answer.short:
$\angle AOB=2(\beta-\alpha)=2\angle APB$.

Subtract the exterior angles at $O$.
answer.worked:
Since $PO$ is produced to $X$, the exterior-angle theorem gives $\angle XOB=2\beta$ in $\triangle OPB$ and $\angle XOA=2\alpha$ in $\triangle OPA$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=\angle XOB-\angle XOA\\\angle AOB&=2\beta-2\alpha\\\angle AOB&=2(\beta-\alpha)\\\angle AOB&=2\angle APB.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked: $AO=OB$ because $O$ is the midpoint of $AB$, and $PO=OQ$ by construction. Thus diagonals $AB$ and $PQ$ bisect each other at $O$, so $APBQ$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, explain why $APBQ$ is a rectangle.

answer.short: It is a parallelogram with a right angle.
answer.worked: $\angle APB=90^\circ$ is given. A parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle, so $APBQ$ is a rectangle.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, explain why $AO=BO=PO$ and why the circle with diameter $AB$ passes through $P$.

answer.short: $AO=BO=PO$, since a rectangle’s diagonals are equal and bisect each other. The circle has centre $O$ and radius $OP$, so it passes through $P$.

The diagonals of rectangle $APBQ$ are equal and bisect each other, so $AB=PQ$ and
$$AO=BO=\frac{AB}{2}=\frac{PQ}{2}=PO.$$
The circle with diameter $AB$ has centre $O$ and radius $AO$. Since $OP=AO$, the point $P$ lies on this circle.

content.prompt: (An application of the angle at the centre and circumference theorem) A horse is travelling around a circular track at a constant speed. A punter standing at the very edge of the track is following him with binoculars. Explain why the punter’s binoculars are rotating at a constant rate.

answer.short: In equal times the horse covers equal arcs. Each angle turned through by the binoculars is half the corresponding angle at the centre, so equal times give equal rotations.
answer.worked:
Constant speed around the circular track means the horse covers equal arcs in equal time intervals, giving equal angles at the centre.

For each such arc, the angle through which the punter turns the binoculars is the angle at the circumference, which is half the corresponding angle at the centre. Therefore the binoculars turn through equal angles in equal time intervals and rotate at a constant rate.

children.prompt: A chord subtends an angle of $90^\circ$ at the centre of a circle of radius $12$ cm.

children.label: i
children.prompt: How long is the chord?

answer.worked: The two radii and chord form a right-angled isosceles triangle. Thus chord length $=\sqrt{12^2+12^2}=12\sqrt2\text{ cm}\approx17.0\text{ cm}$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: How far is the midpoint of the chord from the centre?

answer.worked: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. Its half-length is $6\sqrt2$, so the distance is $\sqrt{12^2-(6\sqrt2)^2}=6\sqrt2\text{ cm}\approx8.5\text{ cm}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: In a circle of radius $20$ cm, the midpoint of a chord is $16$ cm from the centre.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: How long is the chord?

answer.worked: The midpoint-to-centre line is perpendicular to the chord. Half the chord is $\sqrt{20^2-16^2}=12$ cm, so the chord is $24$ cm.

children.label: iv
children.prompt: What angle does the chord subtend at the centre, correct to one decimal place?

answer.worked: The midpoint line bisects the central angle. Its half-angle satisfies $\sin\theta=12/20$, so the whole angle is $2\sin^{-1}(12/20)\approx73.7^\circ$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: In a circle of radius $10$ cm, a chord has length $16$ cm.

children.label: v
children.prompt: What is the perpendicular distance from the chord to the centre?

answer.worked: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving half-length $8$ cm. Hence distance $=\sqrt{10^2-8^2}=6$ cm.

children.label: vi
children.prompt: What angle does the chord subtend at the centre, correct to one decimal place?

answer.worked: Half the central angle satisfies $\sin\theta=8/10$, so the whole angle is $2\sin^{-1}(8/10)\approx106.3^\circ$.

content.prompt: Let AB be an interval with midpoint M, and let P be a point in the plane not on AB.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that if P is equidistant from A and B, then P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

answer.short: P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
answer.worked: Join PA, PB and PM. PA=PB is given, AM=BM since M is the midpoint, and PM is common. Therefore $\triangle PAM\equiv\triangle PBM$ (SSS). Matching angles AMP and BMP are equal and sum to $180^\circ$, so each is $90^\circ$. Thus PM is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Conversely, prove that if P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, then P is equidistant from A and B.

answer.worked: Since P lies on the perpendicular bisector, $\angle PMA=\angle PMB=90^\circ$. Also AM=BM and PM is common. Thus $\triangle PAM\equiv\triangle PBM$ (SAS), giving PA=PB.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use parts a and b to prove that a circle has only one centre.

answer.short: Two non-parallel chord bisectors meet at the unique centre.
answer.worked: Choose three distinct points A,B,C on the circle. Any centre is equidistant from A and B, and from B and C. By parts a and b, it lies on both perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC. The chords are non-parallel, so the bisectors have only one intersection. The circle therefore has only one centre in its plane.

children.label: d
children.prompt: For these questions you will need to think in three dimensions.

children.label: i
children.prompt: A circle is drawn on a piece of paper that lies flat on the table. Is there any other point in three-dimensional space, other than the centre of the circle, that is equidistant from all the points on the circle?

answer.short: Yes: every point on the perpendicular line through the centre.
answer.worked: Let O be the centre, r the radius and P any point on the line through O perpendicular to the paper. For any point X on the circle, triangle POX is right-angled and $PX^2=PO^2+r^2$, independent of X. Thus every such P is equidistant from all points on the circle.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What geometrical object is formed by taking, in three dimensions, the set of all points that are a fixed distance from a given point?

answer.worked: Points at fixed positive distance r from a given point form a sphere of radius r centred at that point.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: What geometrical object is formed by taking, in three dimensions, the set of all points that are a fixed distance from a given line?

answer.worked: Every cross-section perpendicular to the given line is a circle with the fixed radius, so the locus is an infinite circular cylinder.

children.label: iv
children.prompt: What geometrical object is formed by taking, in three dimensions, the set of all points that are a fixed distance from a given interval?

answer.short: A cylindrical surface with hemispherical ends.
answer.worked: For points whose closest point lies inside the interval, the fixed-distance locus is a cylindrical surface. Beyond each endpoint the nearest point is that endpoint, giving a hemispherical end. Together they form a capsule-shaped surface.

children.label: v
children.prompt: What geometrical object is formed by taking, in three dimensions, the set of all points that are equidistant from the endpoints of an interval?

answer.short: The perpendicular-bisector plane of the interval.
answer.worked: A point equidistant from the two endpoints lies in the plane through the midpoint perpendicular to the interval; conversely every point of that plane has equal endpoint distances by Pythagoras.

children.prompt: How could you find the centre of a sphere?

answer.worked: Choose four non-coplanar points A,B,C,D on the sphere. Construct the plane perpendicular to each of AB, AC and AD through its midpoint. The centre is equidistant from all four points and lies on all three planes; their unique intersection is the centre.

content.prompt: Find the values of x, y and θ correct to two decimal places, where tangents are drawn at S and T.

spec.description: Circle centre O; O,A,B collinear in that order, OT radius5 and tangent TB12. OA=x, AB=y, angle TBO=theta. No added right-angle mark.
spec.answerVisibility: Original supplied givens and targets only; no derived numerical values or proof conclusions.

answer.worked:
Since OA and OT are radii, $x=5$. Radius OT is perpendicular to tangent TB.
$$\begin{align*}OB&=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13\\y&=AB=13-5=8\\\tan\theta&=\frac5{12}\\\theta&\approx22.62^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.answerVisibility: Original supplied givens and targets only; no derived numerical values or proof conclusions.

answer.worked:
The radius is $4$, and $OP=OA+AP=4+8=12$. Since OS is perpendicular to PS,
$$\begin{align*}x^2&=12^2-4^2=128\\x&=\sqrt{128}\approx11.31.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The tangents at the four points P, Q, R and S on a circle form a quadrilateral ABCD. Prove that $AB+CD=AD+BC$.

spec.description: Tangential quadrilateral ABCD; contacts P on AB,Q on BC,R on CD,S on DA. No equality marks supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Original supplied givens and targets only; no derived numerical values or proof conclusions.

answer.short: $AB+CD=AD+BC$. Replace each side by its two tangent segments and use equal tangents from each vertex.
answer.worked:
Tangents from each external point are equal: $AP=AS$, $BP=BQ$, $CQ=CR$ and $DR=DS$. Thus
$$\begin{align*}AB+CD&=AP+PB+CR+RD\\&=AS+BQ+CQ+SD\\&=AD+BC.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked: Matching parts of the congruent triangles give $PS=PT$, $\angle SPO=\angle TPO$, and $\angle SOP=\angle TOP$. Hence OP bisects both the angle between the tangents and the angle between OS and OT.

$$\text{Area of triangle}=\frac12\times(\text{perimeter of triangle})\times(\text{radius of circle}).$$

children.prompt: Use congruence to prove that $IR=IP$, and that $IP=IQ$.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle BRI$ and $\triangle BPI$, $\angle RBI=\angle PBI$ (angle bisector), $\angle BRI=\angle BPI=90^\circ$, and $BI$ is common. Thus the triangles are congruent (AAS), so $IR=IP$.

Similarly, $\triangle CPI\cong\triangle CQI$ (AAS: the angle at $C$ is bisected, both feet are right angles and $CI$ is common). Therefore $IP=IQ$.

answer.worked: Right triangles $ARI$ and $AQI$ have the common hypotenuse $AI$ and equal legs $IR=IQ$ from part a. They are congruent (RHS), so $\angle RAI=\angle QAI$. Thus $IA$ is the third angle bisector and all three pass through $I$.

children.prompt: Prove that $C$, $K$, $H$ and $L$ are concyclic.

answer.short: Both $K$ and $L$ lie on the circle with diameter $CH$.
answer.worked: $\angle CKH=90^\circ$ because $AK\perp BC$, and $\angle CLH=90^\circ$ because $BL\perp AC$. By the converse of the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem, $K$ and $L$ both lie on the circle with diameter $CH$. Hence $C,K,H,L$ are concyclic.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Let $\angle ACM=\theta$. Prove that $\angle AKL=\theta$.

answer.worked: From part a, $\angle HKL=\angle HCL$ (angles subtended by chord $HL$). Since $A,H,K$ are collinear and $C,H,M$ and $C,L,A$ are collinear as shown, $\angle AKL=\angle HCL=\angle ACM=\theta$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that $B$, $K$, $L$ and $A$ are concyclic, and hence prove that $\angle ABL=\theta$.

answer.worked: $\angle AKB=\angle ALB=90^\circ$, so $K$ and $L$ lie on the circle with diameter $AB$. Thus $A,B,K,L$ are concyclic. Angles subtended by chord $AL$ give $\angle ABL=\angle AKL=\theta$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence, prove that $CM$ is an altitude of the triangle. That is, we have proved that the three altitudes are concurrent.

answer.short: $CM\perp AB$, so the three altitudes meet at $H$.

content.prompt:
Euler discovered a wonderful theorem that the Greeks had missed:

The orthocentre, the centroid and the circumcentre of a triangle are collinear, with the centroid dividing the interval joining the orthocentre and circumcentre in the ratio $2:1$.

(This line is called the Euler line.)

Note: The centroid is the point of intersection of the medians of a triangle, which are the lines drawn from any vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side.

Let $O$ and $G$ be the circumcentre and centroid, respectively, of $\triangle ABC$. Draw $OG$ and produce it to a point $M$, such that $OG:GM=1:2$.

children.prompt: Let $F$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Use the fact that the centroid, $G$, divides the median $AF$ in the ratio $2:1$ to prove that $\triangle GOF$ is similar to $\triangle GMA$.

answer.worked: The construction gives $GM/GO=2$, and the centroid property gives $GA/GF=2$. Also $\angle OGF=\angle MGA$ (vertically opposite angles). Hence $\triangle GOF\sim\triangle GMA$ (SAS).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, prove that $M$ lies on the altitude from $A$.

answer.worked: The similarity gives $\angle OFG=\angle MAG$, so $OF\parallel AM$ (equal alternate angles on transversal $AF$). Since $O$ is the circumcentre and $F$ is the midpoint of chord $BC$, $OF\perp BC$. Thus $AM\perp BC$, so $M$ lies on the altitude from $A$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that point $M$ is the point $H$ constructed in Question 3.

answer.worked: The same argument using the medians from $B$ and $C$ shows that $BM\perp AC$ and $CM\perp AB$. The point $M$ therefore lies on all three altitudes. Their common intersection is the point $H$ from Question 3, so $M=H$. Thus $O,G,H$ are collinear, with $OG:GH=1:2$ for the construction shown.

answer.worked: Since $APCB$ is cyclic, $\angle ABC+\angle APC=180^\circ$. The hypothesis gives $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$. Subtracting the common angle yields $\angle APC=\angle ADC$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $AA'=BB'$.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the intersection of the indirect tangents. Tangents from the same external point have equal lengths, so $MA=MB$ and $MA'=MB'$. Since $M$ lies between the circles,
$$AA'=AM+MA'=BM+MB'=BB'.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that $AA'=XY$.

answer.worked:
Equal tangent lengths from $X$ give $XC=XA$ and $XC'=XA'$. From $Y$, $YC=YB$ and $YC'=YB'$.

Using the order shown on the direct and indirect tangents,
$$\begin{align*}XY&=XA+AA'-YC',\\XY&=YB'+BB'-XC.\end{align*}$$
Adding and substituting the equal tangent lengths gives
$$2XY=AA'+BB'=2AA'.$$
Therefore $XY=AA'$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Describe what happens when the two circles are touching each other externally.

answer.short: The two indirect tangents merge into the common tangent at the contact point; $AA'=BB'=XY=0$.
answer.worked: At external contact the paired contact points of both indirect tangents coincide at the touching point. The two indirect tangents become the same common tangent there, so $A=A'=B=B'$ and $X=Y$. Consequently all three lengths are zero.

content.prompt: Two circles intersect at $A$ and $B$. A straight line passing through $A$ meets the two circles respectively at $C$ and $D$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that any two triangles $CBD$ formed in this way are similar.

answer.short: The corresponding angles at $C$ and $D$ are fixed circle angles, so the triangles are similar (AA).
answer.worked: For the nondegenerate triangles in the construction, the angle at $C$ is determined by the fixed chord $AB$ in the first circle, and the angle at $D$ is determined by the same chord in the second circle. The straight line through $A$ identifies the corresponding chord rays. These two corresponding angles are constant as the line varies, so any two triangles $CBD$ are similar (AA).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Which of these triangles has the larger area?

answer.short: The largest triangle is obtained when $BC$ and $BD$ are diameters, equivalently when $CD\perp AB$ at $A$.
answer.worked: Since the triangles are similar, their areas increase with the square of a corresponding side. The chord $BC$ is greatest when it is a diameter of the first circle. Then $\angle BAC=90^\circ$, so the variable line through $A$ is perpendicular to $AB$. In the second circle, $\angle BAD=90^\circ$ as well, so $BD$ is also a diameter. This configuration therefore gives the greatest area.

If $\triangle ABC$ has side lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$, prove that:
$$\frac{2\times(\text{Area of }\triangle ABC)}{abc}=\frac{\sin C}{c}=\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{\sin B}{b}.$$

answer.worked:
Let $\Delta$ be the area of $\triangle ABC$. The area formula with each included angle gives
$$2\Delta=ab\sin C=bc\sin A=ca\sin B.$$
All three side lengths are positive. Dividing by $abc$ yields
$$\frac{2\Delta}{abc}=\frac{\sin C}{c}=\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{\sin B}{b}.$$

entries.description:
As we can see from the fourth example from the previous page, when the arc is a semicircle, the angle at the centre is 180° and the angle at the circumference is 90°. You will recognise that this is precisely the situation covered by Thales’ theorem, which is thus a special case of our new theorem.
Thus, the two theorems are an excellent example of a theorem and its generalisation. This situation occurs routinely throughout mathematics. For example, the cosine rule can be thought of as a generalisation of Pythagoras’ theorem.

entries.description:
Proof:
Let ABC be a triangle.
Let M be the midpoint of AB, and let N be the midpoint of BC.
Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet at O, and join AO, BO and CO.
Then △AOM ≡ △BOM (SAS)
so AO = BO (matching sides of congruent triangles),
and △CON ≡ △BON (SAS)
so CO = BO (matching sides of congruent triangles),
so AO = BO = CO
Hence, O is equidistant from A, B and C, so the circle with centre O and radius AO passes through A, B and C.

entries.description:
Common tangents and touching circles
The five diagrams below show all the ways in which two circles of different radii can intersect. Start with the smaller circle inside the larger, and move it slowly to the right. Notice that the two circles can intersect at two, one or no points.
The various lines are all the common tangents to the two circles. There are 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 common tangents in the five successive diagrams.
In the second and fourth diagrams, the two circles touch each other, and they have a common tangent at the point of contact.

entries.description:
Here is a form of the sine rule that shows its connection with the circumcircle of a triangle.
In any triangle ABC, a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R,
where R is the radius of the circumcircle of triangle ABC. Assume that A is acute.
Draw the circumcircle of △ABC, and let O be the circumcentre.

presentation.requiredResponseSpace: Student drawing space for the circumcircle and triangle; proof space for the following parts.

entries.description: The extended sine rule and the definition of R as the circumradius are embedded in question 1.
Hence, prove that a/sin A = 2R.
Prove the result when ∠A is obtuse.

Circle with centre O and inscribed triangle ABC. A is upper left, B is at the left end of a horizontal diameter BP, P is at its right end, and C is lower right. Chord BC is labelled a. Triangle sides and circle are blue; diameter BP and chord PC are red dashed lines; O is marked by a red point on BP.
entries.presentation: Supplied diagram sits to the right of question 1. Preserve the diameter relationship, all labels and the auxiliary segment PC; dimensions are unspecified.

entries.description:
Prove that: In any triangle ABC, the bisectors of the vertex angles are concurrent, and the resulting incentre is the centre of a circle that touches all sides of the triangle.
Let the angle bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at I, and draw IA. Draw the perpendiculars IP, IQ and IR to the sides BC, CA and AB, respectively.
Use congruence to prove that IR = IP, and that IP = IQ.
Use congruence to prove that IA bisects ∠A.
Why does the circle with centre I and radius IR touch all three sides of the triangle?

Triangle ABC with A above, B left and C lower right. BI and CI meet at interior point I. At B, the two angles separated by BI are each labelled β; at C, the two angles separated by CI are each labelled γ. R lies on AB, Q on AC and P on BC. Red dashed segments IR, IQ and IP meet those sides at marked right angles. AI is also red dashed. Triangle sides and bisectors BI and CI are blue.
entries.presentation: Supplied diagram to the right of question 2; preserve perpendicular feet and equal-angle labels.

entries.description:
Prove that: In any triangle ABC, the altitudes are concurrent (their intersection is called the orthocentre of the triangle).
Let the altitudes AK and BL meet at H. Draw CH and produce it to meet AB at M.
Prove that C, K, H and L are concyclic.
Let ∠ACM = θ. Prove that ∠AKL = θ.
Prove that B, K, L and A are concyclic, and hence prove that ∠ABL = θ.
Hence, prove that CM is an altitude of the triangle. That is, we have proved that the three altitudes are concurrent.

Triangle ABC with horizontal base BC, A above near B, K on BC and L on AC. Blue altitudes AK and BL intersect at H; right-angle markers show AK perpendicular to BC and BL perpendicular to AC. M lies on AB, with red dashed CM passing through H. Red dashed KL is also drawn. The angle between CA and CM at C is labelled θ.
entries.presentation: Supplied diagram to the right of question 3. Preserve auxiliary KL and the incidence C–H–M.

entries.description:
Euler discovered a wonderful theorem that the Greeks had missed:
The orthocentre, the centroid and the circumcentre of a triangle are collinear, with the centroid dividing the interval joining the orthocentre and circumcentre in the ratio 2 : 1.
(This line is called the Euler line.)
Note: The centroid is the point of intersection of the medians of a triangle, which are the lines drawn from any vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Let O and G be the circumcentre and centroid, respectively, of △ABC. Draw OG and produce it to a point, M, such that OG : GM = 1 : 2.

presentation.continuation: Question begins here and continues beyond this page.

entries.description: Euler-line theorem, name of the Euler line, and definition of centroid and medians are embedded in question 4.

Triangle ABC with A above, C at the left of horizontal base CB and B at its right. F is the midpoint of CB, indicated by matching double ticks on CF and FB. Median AF passes through G. O, G and M are collinear, with G between O and M; AM is drawn. OF meets CB at a marked right angle. All construction lines are blue.
entries.presentation: Supplied diagram to the right of question 4; preserve midpoint marks, perpendicular OF and the O–G–M order.

entries.description:

Suppose that two intervals AB and CD intersect at M, and that AM × BM = CM × DM. Then the points A, B, C and D are concyclic.
Draw the circle through the points A, B and C. Let CD, produced if necessary, meet the circle at P.

entries.description: Prove that PM × CM = AM × BM.

entries.description:
Take two non-intersecting circles in the plane with centres O and O′. Draw two indirect common tangents AA′ and BB′, and one direct tangent CC′, where A, B and C lie on the first circle, and A′, B′ and C′ lie on the second circle.
Produce AA′ and BB′ to meet CC′ at X and Y.

entries.description: Prove that AA′ = BB′.
Prove that AA′ = XY.
Describe what happens when the two circles are touching each other externally.

Two disjoint circles, smaller on the left with centre O and larger on the right with centre O′. Indirect common tangents AA′ and BB′ cross at M between the circles. A is upper right and B lower right on the left circle; A′ is lower left and B′ upper left on the right circle. A sloping direct common tangent touches the circles at C and C′ above their centres. It meets AA′ at X near C and BB′ at Y near B′. Centres and six tangency points are marked red; circles and tangent lines are blue.
entries.presentation: Preserve all labels, tangencies, intersections and relative arrangement. M is labelled in the diagram although not introduced in the printed stem.
